Before he knew how to read, neuroscientist David Hubel learned to play the piano. In his memoir, the Nobel Prize winner said his main teacher, a Montreal organist, gave him “a love of Bach that I would not trade for any amount of success in science.” For the rest of his life, he played for about an hour every day.
p

Hubel’s memoir is part of a treasure trove of autobiographies written by prominent neuroscientists that the Society for Neuroscience has been compiling for more than 30 years. The 14th volume of the series, “The History of Neuroscience in Autobiography,” was published earlier this month.
p

The series includes contributions from 195 scientists, 8 of whom are Nobel Prize winners. Some of the memoirists are founders of the field—Sir Alan Hodgkin, Andrew Huxley and Marian Diamond—and others are more recent leaders, such as Ben Barres, Eve Marder and Huda Zoghbi.
p

The editors of the series, Larry Squire and Thomas Albright, say they commission chapters based on recommendations from the society’s leadership committees. Squire, emeritus distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, San Diego, began the series during his 1993-1994 term as society president; Albright, distinguished professor emeritus at the Salk Institute, joined as co-editor beginning with the ninth volume.
p

Squire and Albright spoke with The Transmitter about why the personal stories of neuroscience matter, their favorite chapters from the series, and what they have learned from reading about the lives of hundreds of neuroscientists.
p
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
p
The Transmitter: What was the motivation for creating this autobiography series?
p

Larry Squire: Well, I knew that there was a similar effort done in the psychology discipline. So when I served a term as president of the Society for Neuroscience, I proposed that we do something similar because the chapters were so interesting about the nature of the work that had been done—false steps and lucky steps, and so on. Plus, neuroscience is moving so fast, and so many new techniques are coming along that we’ve seen the field change a couple times within our own generation. If you look at the first couple volumes we have, you see the difference between what’s being done then and what’s being done now.
p
TT: What can an autobiography capture that a traditional scientific account would leave out?
p

Thomas Albright: We’re pretty explicit when we invite people that these are not scientific retrospectives. They’re not intended to go into great detail about the science. They’re more looking at the figures—mentors, colleagues, students, institutions—that have played an important role in their lives and the development of their career, and how those relationships sparked new ideas or led to certain interpretations that might not otherwise have happened.
p
LS: Even the first 10 pages of each volume are illuminating because they explain how the person found their way into the field and what kind of specialization they had.
p
TT: Why is it important to record and preserve the personal side of neuroscience?
p

TA: It’s embedded in the preface of the first volume: Science is done by people, and people are interesting creatures. They’re highly social. They’re making important decisions, and you can’t help but wonder, Why do people do these things? Why do they go in the directions they go over the course of their lives? The path to enormous success is what we’re trying to capture here, and how do you get there? That’s what this is about.
p

LS: It helps for later scholarship as well, to settle issues that become important about priority, or the details of what happened. In Volume 2 we have a marvelous chapter by Brenda Milner from Montreal, who’s now 108 years old. And in her chapter, she actually settles some issues that have come up as her work became more important in her field. People step in all the wrong places sometimes; they get facts wrong. But her memoir clears it all up for everybody.
p
TT: Which chapters are your favorites?
p

TA: The first couple of volumes include heroes of the 20th-century neuroscience community. It’s just remarkable that all this is documented. I study the visual system; David Hubel—who was really my model, growing up, for how to study the brain—is in Volume 1. There’s one in the latest volume that was not about a field that I have much familiarity with, but it’s just beautifully written, and that’s by David Anderson.
p

LS: And in a few cases, we read marvelous stories of the author’s growing up and their parents. I remember in particular the chapter by Solomon Snyder, who’s a luminary in the field of neuroscience. He told magnificent stories about his parents. His mother was apparently a national champion of writing contests, and she had a kitchen filled with appliances she had won.
p
We have lots of memories of individual chapters that are pretty remarkable. I could go on forever.
p

TA: Yeah, there’s so many of them. I recently learned that Gerry Fischbach died. I knew Gerry well. He was a non-resident fellow for many years at the Salk Institute when I was a young, up-and-coming neuroscientist. I knew him to be a wonderful and encouraging person, so I read his autobiography. I developed this relationship with him as a result of what I read, and we discussed all sorts of things.
p

In fact, more generally, I know most of these people, and many of them personally, but as a result of reading their autobiographies, I feel like I’ve gained some intimacy into their lives, which is kind of a strange thing. And I feel like in some cases they’re like old friends, even though I’ve never been to their house, I’ve never had dinner with them. I just know their work, and I’ve read their autobiography. It actually transforms the way I feel about them, which is, I guess, the point.
p
TT: You’ve edited the life stories of 195 scientists. What themes stick out to you? Has anything surprised you?
p

TA: There are a lot of different ways people get into science. David Anderson, at the outset of his chapter, says that he never had anything in his childhood that would have led anyone to expect him to become a scientist. He had lots of other interests, and somehow, when he went off to college, the social environment he was in steered him toward science. He’s a brilliant man and ended up doing remarkable things. And there are other people who were taking apart their transistor radios when they were kids, or identifying all the different kinds of frogs in the yard.
p

LS: We had a lot of confessions and material that we wouldn’t have expected to show up in an autobiography. We had a descent into alcoholism described in detail by one of the early authors. We had a European scientist who unexpectedly spent most of his chapter making priority claims about his work and showing that he did something before somebody else. I thought it was a little peculiar, but we published it as it was because we give our authors much latitude. But two years later, he won the Nobel Prize. So I guess he had a point.
